title: It Takes a Little Nerve to Write the First Rough Note
summary: Why the first rough note is the hardest one to write, what Paul Graham and Anne Lamott say about bad first drafts, and a four-line template to get a messy idea down.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
You walk out of a code review with half a thought. Something like: we only explain a decision once it’s already expensive to change. It isn’t an idea yet. It’s barely a sentence. So you open your notes app, stare at the empty page for a bit, and close it again. You’ll write it up properly once it’s clearer.

That “once it’s clearer” moment almost never shows up. This post is about the first rough note: why it feels harder than it should, what it does for your thinking, and a four-line template that gets you past the blank page.

Why a blank page feels risky

In your head, an idea feels finished because nothing is testing it. Write it down and the gaps show up right away: the wording is clumsy, the order is off, the example is weaker than you remembered. Paul Graham says it plainly in Putting Ideas into Words: writing about something, even something you know well, usually shows you that you didn’t know it as well as you thought. He calls putting ideas into words “a severe test.”

That’s the scary part, and it’s also the useful part. A thought that only lives in your head has no version history. You can’t diff it, reorder it, hand it to a teammate or link it to another idea. It just replays, sounding a little more convincing each time. Once it’s on the page, it becomes something you can actually work on.

Let the first version be bad

Anne Lamott named her book on writing, Bird by Bird, after a family story. Her older brother, ten at the time, had had three months to write a report on birds, and it was due the next day. He sat at the kitchen table close to tears, frozen by how big the job looked. Their father sat down next to him, put an arm around his shoulder and said: “Bird by bird, buddy. Just take it bird by bird.”

A first note works the same way. Nobody is waiting on the final article, the perfect proposal or the airtight argument today. The page only needs one sentence that makes the next sentence possible. Keep the bar low on purpose, low enough that your ego doesn’t feel any need to defend it.

Engineers already do this all the time

Watch how work moves on a team. A design discussion stays foggy until someone sketches the first ugly box-and-arrow diagram. A requirement feels obvious until someone tries to write the acceptance criteria and finds three questions nobody has answered. The first artifact is rarely pretty. Its job is to give the conversation something concrete to push on.

Some of the best-known writing habits in engineering are built on exactly that. Malte Ubl’s write-up of design docs at Google describes them as relatively informal, and the first benefit he lists is catching design issues early, while changes are still cheap. Michael Nygard keeps each architecture decision record to one or two pages, because, as he puts it, nobody ever reads large documents. Both habits work because the writing shows up early and short, while the thinking can still change.

A rough note can be four lines

If the blank page keeps winning, use a template so plain it’s almost boring:

  • What happened?
  • What did I notice?
  • Why does it matter?
  • What might I try next time?

Four half-answers are plenty. Here’s the code review thought from the top, written that way: “Payment PR review. We only explained why we picked the queue after someone asked for a rollback. Explaining late costs more than explaining early. Next time, add two lines of ‘why’ to the PR description.” That takes about a minute. Later it might grow into a decision record, a better PR template or a blog post. It might also sit in your notes forever, and that’s fine too. It has already kept the lesson from slipping away.

A rule of thumb

Write the first note for tomorrow’s you. An audience can come later. Tomorrow’s you only needs enough context to remember what today’s you noticed.

Go easy on other people’s drafts

The fear behind rough writing is usually the fear of being seen too early. We’d like people to meet our finished thinking and skip the awkward middle. Yet almost every useful idea has an awkward middle, and a polished final doc hides plenty of crossed-out sentences and wrong turns.

So when a teammate shares an early draft, try not to grade it like a final one. Ask questions that help it grow. What are you trying to protect here? Which constraint matters most? What example would make this click for me? Teams that read drafts this way get to see ideas while they’re still cheap to change, and people stop hiding their work until it has set hard.

Try it this week

Pick one thought that keeps coming back after a meeting, a bug or a review. Give it four rough lines today, before you decide whether it’s worth keeping. If you’re curious what happens when you keep going, there’s a post on what a month of small notes shows you, and another on coming back to an old note months later.

faqs.q: Why is the first draft so hard to write?
faqs.a: In your head an idea feels complete because nothing tests it. Writing it down shows the gaps right away. Paul Graham calls putting ideas into words a severe test, since writing usually shows you that you knew the topic less well than you thought. That discomfort is the useful part.

faqs.q: What should a rough note include?
faqs.a: Four short answers are enough: what happened, what you noticed, why it matters and what you might try next time. Clumsy is fine. It takes about a minute.

faqs.q: How does this apply to engineering work?
faqs.a: Design docs and architecture decision records work the same way. Malte Ubl lists catching design issues early, while changes are cheap, as the first benefit of design docs at Google, and Michael Nygard keeps each decision record to one or two pages. Short and early beats long and late.

faqs.q: How should I respond to a teammate's rough draft?
faqs.a: Read it as thinking in progress and ask questions that help it grow: what they are trying to protect, which constraint matters most, what example would make it clearer. Grading it like a final document teaches people to hide drafts until it is too late to change them.
